JourKnows PH Explainer · October 2026

Paris is
on its feet.

Students, workers, and drivers are filling the streets of France again. The anger is about school budgets, fuel, and the cost of staying afloat. If it sounds familiar, it should.

01 · Right now

A movement that moves in waves.

Since late September, strikes and marches have rolled through France. High school blockades spread across regions, universities joined, and the Yellow Vests were called back for October 17.

03 · It has been a long time

237 years of a nation that refuses to stay quiet.

France did not just protest. It made protest part of its identity.

04 · The long view

Years since 1789

Each wave answered the same question: who pays when the state and the market squeeze ordinary people?

05 · Rizal in Paris

The city that taught him what a people could demand.

Rizal reached Paris twice. In 1885, fresh from medical studies in Madrid, he trained in an ophthalmology clinic. He returned in early 1889, when Noli Me Tángere had already marked him as a danger to Spanish authorities.

That year he spent his days at the Bibliothèque Nationale, annotating Antonio de Morga’s Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas. The project argued that Filipinos had a civilization before Spain arrived. It was published in Paris in 1890.

Paris was also a stage. The Exposition Universelle opened on May 6, 1889, under the brand-new Eiffel Tower, to mark one hundred years since the Revolution. Rizal watched a republic celebrate the overthrow of a king while his own country remained a colony.

Among Filipino friends such as Juan Luna, he helped form the Kidlat Club and Indios Bravos, circles meant to prove that Filipinos could excel in letters, science, and art.

06 · The lodge

Liberty, equality, fraternity, carried across an ocean.

Rizal joined Freemasonry in Madrid in the 1880s. Paris, where lodges stood with the Republic against clerical power, was one of its centers. The lodges spoke a dangerous language for a colony ruled with the friar’s sermon: reason over decree, schooling free of the church, equality regardless of birth, and brotherhood across borders.

The reformers around him, including Marcelo H. del Pilar and Graciano López Jaena, moved in the same circles. Their paper, La Solidaridad, argued for Filipino rights from Europe between 1889 and 1895.

Many historians trace a thread from these lodges to the Katipunan, founded in 1892 by Andrés Bonifacio. Its secret initiation, oaths, and brotherhood echo lodge ritual, though scholars debate how far the influence ran. What is clear is the shift: reform petitions in Madrid became revolution in Manila.

07 · The thread

From Paris to EDSA to the Trillion Peso March.

An idea that begins in a library in Paris does not stay there. It changes shape, and returns whenever Filipinos ask who the state belongs to.

08 · Why Filipinos must care

This is not someone else’s fight.

We share the same squeeze

Fuel hikes, frozen wages, and rising prices drive French anger. Filipino households know the pump price and the grocery bill just as well.

Youth and schools

French students are marching for classroom resources. Our campuses face crowded rooms and tight budgets, and campus press is often the first to say so.

Accountability is universal

Filipinos filled the streets against flood control corruption. The question is the same: where did the public money go?

Our people are there

Filipinos live, study, and work across France and Europe. Strikes ground flights, halt trains, and shape OFW livelihoods.

Our history rhymes

Rizal and the Propagandists absorbed Europe’s revolutionary ideas. Liberté, égalité, fraternité echoes in our own struggle for dignity.

09 · The question
When a people stops asking permission to be heard, the whole world learns what is possible.

France has asked its question for 237 years. The Philippines has asked its own, from 1896 to EDSA to today. Watching Paris is a way of learning how to ask ours louder.
